rappel_detail.notes: First rappel off the upper south saddle down the slabby trough, before reaching the Great Chimney.

rappel_detail.pull: About 75 ft of drop, so a 60 m rope doubled covers it. A party on 25 m ropes was left roughly five metres short and had to break the chimney into two rappels.
rappel_detail.notes: 75-ft rappel through the Great Chimney cannonhole (a narrow squeeze slot).
hazards: The tunnel is a real squeeze — packs come off and get pushed through ahead of you, which is exactly why parties take the lip instead
Going over the lip loads the chockstone edge: a block there has split under rope tension and run down the chimney, striking both climbers of one party
Anchors through the chimney are aged natural slings, described by more than one party as questionable, and the chimney funnels everything that comes loose
rappel_detail.station: The highest chockstone in the Great Chimney. There are two ways to rig it: through the low keyhole/tunnel under the chockstone, which is the recommended line and gives a low-angle drop, or over the lip of the chockstone, which is overhanging.

rappel_detail.notes: 75-ft rappel off a mid-chimney chockstone, ending at a narrow ledge; party then traverses back to the high southeast notch.
hazards: The landing is a narrow exposed ledge, not easy ground, and it is where the descent changes direction
Anything dislodged in the chimney runs a long way; parties on this face have sent rock all the way down to the glacier below
rappel_detail.station: A slung chockstone partway down the chimney. The rappel ends on a narrow, exposed ledge — from there parties traverse back to the high southeast notch rather than continuing straight down the chimney line.

rappel_detail.notes: Rappel down the snow/rock gully, passing through a snow cannonhole halfway down.
hazards: Moats are open on both sides of the snow fin at the hole
rappel_detail.station: Rappel down the snow/rock gully from the high southeast notch. Halfway down the line threads a second cannonhole — this one a hole through a tall snow fin.

rappel_detail.pull: Pull from as far out of the cleft as the ground allows, and treat a spare cord or a stuck-rope plan as part of the rack rather than optional.
rappel_detail.notes: Final rappel through a rock cleft on the southeast rib back to descent terrain; ropes are prone to sticking here (one party sacrificed a rope).
hazards: This is the documented rope-eater on the route: a party's rope jammed on the pull here, resisted every retrieval attempt, and was left on the mountain — in the dark, on the way out
rappel_detail.station: The final rappel drops through a cleft in the rock of the southeast rib back onto walking terrain.

wa_american_border_peak_southeast_face.rappel_count_note: Accounts disagree on the count. One party made three rappels on the way down; another needed just two, starting at the top of the keyhole, to get down. A third account describes five rappels, but that is one party’s descent on two 25 m ropes rather than a list of fixed stations — which is why its lengths (about 23 m / 75 ft) look so precise and why its count disagrees with the others. That party’s final rappel off the southeast rib jammed and they sacrificed a rope; the standard line threads the low keyhole beneath the chockstone for a cleaner pull.
wa_american_border_peak_southeast_face.descent_text: Descend by reversing the Southeast Face/South Ridge line back down to the South AmBo Saddle — the terrain is loose and complex enough that there is no clean walk-off alternative. Expect two to four short rappels through the summit chimney/gully system, with the count depending on party size, rope handling, and which chockstone squeeze you take: the standard, recommended line threads the low "keyhole"/tunnel beneath a large chockstone (pull packs off, push them through, crawl after), giving a clean, low-angle rappel; parties who instead rig over the lip of the chockstone get a harder, overhanging drop and sometimes add an extra rappel to manage it. A single 60m rope, doubled, is sufficient for the individual rappels (each reported at around 75 ft/~23 m), so plan on doubled-strand rappels off a 60m rope rather than needing two ropes. Anchors are entirely natural — slung chockstones and horns with in-place webbing that is often sun-bleached and aged — there are no bolts on this route, so inspect and back up (or replace) any tat you find and carry your own cord/rap rings; at least one party describes sacrificing a rope that got stuck in a rappel crack, so a pull-cord or a stuck-rope contingency is worth planning for. After the last rappel off the southeast rib, downclimb loose 3rd-class terrain back into the red talus bowl, then reverse the long sidehill traverse below Mt. Larrabee back to Gargett Mine and High Pass, and finish on the High Pass Trail to Twin Lakes. Loose rock remains the dominant hazard for the entire descent — keep the party tight through the gullies and budget real time for the tedious traverse back across scree and heather, especially late in the day; parties camped at Gargett Basin typically descend only as far as camp the first evening and walk out to the trailhead the next morning.

wa_argonaut_peak_east_ridge.rappel_count_note: The rappels into the notch are two single-rope rappels, or one on a double rope; their lengths and anchors are not recorded. The descent gully adds one short rappel or belayed downclimb at its chockstone step.

rappel_detail.notes: This table follows the southeast-face ledge line. The other descent involves two rappels on the slabs directly north of the east gully, followed by a traverse along a wet ledge into it. Choose one line before you leave the summit.
rappel_detail.anchor: Natural, and not guaranteed to be in place — you may need to rig the anchor yourself, and one earlier party describes rappelling off a tree with a sling, on the ledge facing southeast. Carry webbing and nuts for this descent.
hazards: No reliable fixed station — arriving expecting one and finding nothing is the failure mode here
You are committing off the summit onto a face on the opposite side of the peak from the couloir you climbed
rappel_detail.station: Head back down from the summit to the upper rock band; the single rappel from there drops onto the ledge on the southeast face.

rappel_detail.anchor: Natural / rigged; an older two-rope description set up at a stopper anchor midway up the southeast face.
hazards: Gully terrain, loose
Anchors may have to be built from nuts and left behind
rappel_detail.station: First of the rappels down the gully lying east of the top of the Northeast Couloir, entered from the southeast-face ledge.

rappel_detail.notes: A third rappel in this gully is described as sometimes necessary, so treat the count as two or three here rather than fixed.
hazards: Loose gully; the transition onto snow at the bottom may need axe and crampons depending on season
rappel_detail.station: Continues down the same gully; the sequence ends on the snow slopes below, from which parties traverse toward the Colchuck-Dragontail notch or glissade the Colchuck Glacier.

wa_argonaut_peak_northeast_couloir.rappel_count_note: The stations follow the usual descent: one rappel to the southeast-face ledge, then down the gully east of the couloir’s top, where two or three single-rope rappels reach the snow, so 3-4 rappels in all. Anchors are natural and not guaranteed to be in place; carry webbing and nuts. The other line, two rappels down slabs north of the east gully off slung blocks and a small tree, then a protected wet-ledge traverse into the gully, is an alternative, not a continuation.

wa_bears_breast_mountain_southwest_face.rappels: 3 single-rope rappels off the summit block (a single 50m rope reaches; a 60m or two 50m ropes are more comfortable for parties of 3+)

rappel_detail.notes: One long rappel, reported as roughly 60 m; some parties found a 60 m rope barely reaches the anchor. Below it, bypass steep snow and waterfall-wet rock to the side and downclimb about two more rope-lengths of steep terrain to the lower basin.
hazards: Check that your rope reaches before committing.
In winter and spring parties downclimb the Dry Creek couloir instead, which is insecure and dangerous.
rappel_detail.station: A notch on the south ridge, reached by reversing the summit ridge over the lower first bump.

wa_big_four_mountain_dry_creek_route.rappels: 1 long rappel (reported as about 60 m) from a notch on the south ridge, then about two rope-lengths of steep downclimbing to the lower basin
wa_big_four_mountain_dry_creek_route.descent_text: Most parties descend the same Dry Creek line they climbed. From the true summit, reverse the summit ridge over the lower (first) bump, then set up a roughly 60-meter rappel from a notch on the south ridge -- some parties have found a 60m rope barely reaches the anchor/chockstone. Below the rappel, bypass steep snow and waterfall-moistened rock to the side, then downclimb roughly two more rope-lengths of steep terrain to regain the lower basin before retracing the approach back across the South Fork Stillaguamish and out to the trailhead. In winter/spring, parties instead downclimb the Dry Creek couloir itself, which parties describe as a genuinely dangerous, insecure downclimb.

rappel_detail.notes: First of two ~200 ft rappels down steep slabs on the West Peak's northwest side; a rope of at least 60m (or two ropes joined) is needed to reach the next stance.
rappel_detail.anchor: gear anchor (nut, per one documented descent)

rappel_detail.notes: Second ~200 ft rappel reaching the approach basin; anchors here are improvised rather than fixed, so carry a small rack/cordage. Some parties finish this descent after dark.
rappel_detail.anchor: gear anchor (piton, per one documented descent)

wa_soviet_route.rappels: Two ~200-ft rappels down slabs on the standard descent
wa_soviet_route.descent_text: From the Southwest Peak (route's high point), traverse the Northeast Ridge to the West Peak — about 2 hours, negotiating a series of gendarmes mostly on 3rd/4th-class ledges, with one short rappel along the way. From the West Peak, descend the northwest side: downclimb talus, then make two rappels of roughly 200 feet each down steep slabs back into the approach basin. Anchors on this descent have historically been improvised rather than fixed — one documented descent used a nut at the top station and a piton at the lower one — so carry a small rack/cordage to build or reinforce anchors rather than counting on hardware being in place. Two 200-ft rappels require a rope of at least 60m (or two ropes joined) to reach each next stance without coming up short. Parties have finished this descent after dark on long summit days, so budget extra time and bring a headlamp. From the bottom of the raps, continue downclimbing talus back to camp near the 7,100' pass, then reverse the terrace descent to Hart Lake and the Railroad Creek Trail back to Holden.

wa_beckey_tate.rappels: Descend the West Route gully: one single-rope rappel from slung blocks at the notch. Rappelling Beckey-Tate itself takes five or six two-rope rappels off slings and trees through loose rock, and most parties avoid it.
wa_beckey_tate.descent_text: Do not plan to rappel the Beckey-Tate line itself — while it's technically possible with two ropes (roughly five or six rappels off slings and trees), the route wanders and holds a lot of large loose rock, making rope-stuck and rockfall risk high; most parties explicitly avoid it. Instead, from the top of the route scramble about 20 ft up and left to reach the notch that separates the south face from the true summit, which stands a few hundred feet higher. To tag it, drop about 150 ft of scree on the far side, cross north into the West Route gully and climb its short pitches to the unprotected 5.6 summit slab (protected by a single old bolt), which is downclimbed or top-roped; then descend the shared gully: two slung-block anchors get you down with one or two single-rope rappels (a 60m rope is sufficient either way) through the steep/loose upper gully, after which it's a scree-and-snow walk/glissade down the gully back to the approach basin, across Early Winters Creek, and out the climbers' trail to the Hairpin Turn. Expect the full descent to take a couple of hours; keep helmets on throughout given the loose rock in the gully.

rappel_detail.pull: Keep both ends clear of the constriction above the wide crack before the last climber pulls - it is the documented rope trap on this descent.
rappel_detail.notes: First rappel of the shared North Face descent line.
hazards: A single 60 m rope does NOT reach the bolts: you finish roughly 10 ft above them and downclimb easy 5th class to get there. A 70 m single is the length that reaches, and is what recent parties recommend
This is the rappel where a party got a rope end stuck in a constriction above a wide crack and had to lead 5.8 back up to free it
rappel_detail.station: The summit anchor - the heavily slung summit boulder - dropping down the upper north face to what is reported to be the only bolted anchor on the whole rappel route. Everything below it is slung natural gear, so this is the one station you can identify with certainty.

rappel_detail.notes: Traverses to reach the next anchor.
rappel_detail.anchor: Bolts to a ledge near a rock arch
hazards: The line does not follow the route, so what you see going down is not what you climbed
rappel_detail.station: Down toward the main ledge system. Parties on two ropes report doubling up and rappelling climber's-left of the climbing line to reach the next station rather than dropping straight down it.

rappel_detail.notes: Drops to a slung horn.
hazards: Ledge-to-ledge rappelling on this face means loose material sitting on every stance above you
rappel_detail.station: One rappel goes from the ledge system down to the ledge at the base of the third pitch.

rappel_detail.notes: Down to scree ledges.
hazards: You have to walk under and past a large block to find this station, so it is not visible from where the previous rappel lands
Traversing a ledge with the ropes still out is where they snag on this descent
rappel_detail.station: From the ledge, cut climber's left to the station, which sits just after you walk back underneath the large block. A station is also reported at the top of pitch 4, reached by a ledge traverse - the ledge is the feature to navigate by, not the fall line.

rappel_detail.notes: Final rappel back to Burgundy Col, 5-10 minutes from Action Potential's own start.
hazards: The notch is the aiming point; below the col the descent continues down loose gullies on foot
rappel_detail.station: The last rappels run down through the sandy terraces to Burgundy Col. From the final stance the rappel route is a straight shot through the obvious notch in the rock below to the ground.

wa_action_potential.rappel_count_note: The five stations are the double-rope count. The same descent is not five rappels for everyone: a party taking many shorter rappels on a single rope logged 9-10 to reverse the route back to Burgundy Col, and a party on two 60 m ropes describes doubling up for the first, one single rappel to the ledge at the bottom of pitch 3, then three more double rappels to the col. Neither is wrong. Action Potential has no rappel line of its own - parties finish into North Face terrain near Burgundy Ledge and take that route's descent. On rope choice, experience differs in a way worth knowing: two ropes are faster, but one party found double ropes on this descent annoying and prone to getting stuck, and recommends a single 70 m instead - a single 60 m leaves you about 10 ft above the only bolted anchor on the route. Per-station distances are not known; the figures given are estimates, not measurements.
wa_action_potential.descent_text: Action Potential tops out in two possible ways, and the descent depends on which finish you take: either climb up past an old bolt to the skyline and ramble class-5.7 terrain to the true summit, or finish by traversing Burgundy Ledge into the standard North Face route. Either way, the descent used by essentially all parties is the North Face's rappel line: with double ropes, plan on 5 rappels from the summit area back down the face — roughly 40m off a heavily slung summit boulder, 55m off bolts to a ledge near a rock arch, 55m off a sling at a constriction to a slung horn, 40m to scree ledges, and a final 60m back to Burgundy Col, 5-10 minutes from Action Potential's own start. Anchors are a mix of slung boulders/horns and fixed bolts; watch for old webbing and be deliberate pulling ropes, since the face has ledges that catch the line. From the base of the last rappel, reverse the Burgundy Col approach to the highway.

rappel_detail.pull: The constriction above the wide crack is the documented rope-eater on this face. Watch where the ends land and keep both strands out of it.
rappel_detail.notes: Drops down the middle of the upper face to a bolted ledge anchor.
hazards: A single 60 m rope comes up about 10 ft short of the bolts and the last of it is an unroped downclimb on easy 5th class; a 70 m single reaches
A party rappelling here got a rope end wedged in a constriction above a wide crack and had to lead 5.8 to recover it
rappel_detail.station: The slung summit boulder, dropping down the upper north face to the only bolted anchor anywhere on this rappel route. Below it every station is slung natural gear, so this is the single anchor you can positively identify.

rappel_detail.notes: Down lichen-covered rock to a large ledge near a rock arch; traverse the ledge to a constriction with slings.
hazards: The rappel line diverges from the climb, so the terrain below you is ground you have not seen
rappel_detail.station: Down toward the main ledge system, rappelling climber's-left of the climbing line rather than straight down it.

rappel_detail.notes: Drops to a horn slung with blue webbing.
hazards: Loose material accumulates on these ledges and sits directly above whoever is next on the rope
rappel_detail.station: One rappel from the ledge system down to the ledge at the bottom of the third pitch.

rappel_detail.notes: Down to broad scree ledges.
hazards: Not visible from where the previous rappel lands - you have to walk under the block to find it
Traversing with ropes deployed is where they hang up here
rappel_detail.station: Cut climber's left from the ledge; the station is just past the point where you walk back underneath the large block. Accounts also describe a station at the top of pitch 4 reached by traversing the ledge - navigate by the ledge and the block, not by looking straight down.

rappel_detail.notes: Final rappel back to Burgundy Col.
hazards: Below the col the descent is loose gullies on foot rather than more rappelling
rappel_detail.station: The remaining rappels run down through the sandy terraces to Burgundy Col; from the last stance the line is a straight shot down through the obvious notch in the rock below to the ground.

wa_ultramega_ok.rappels: 5 double-rope rappels down the North Face rappel line to Burgundy Col; 9-10 shorter rappels on a single rope
wa_ultramega_ok.rappel_count_note: Five stations is the double-rope count. Ultramega OK has no rappel line of its own - it is a Northeast Buttress route that merges into upper North Face terrain, and parties take the North Face descent. The same ground is 9-10 rappels for a party doing many shorter ones on a single rope, and a two-60 party describes it as a doubled first rappel, one single rappel to the ledge at the bottom of pitch 3, then three more double rappels to Burgundy Col - all three counts describe one descent under different rope setups. Rope opinion is genuinely split rather than settled: two ropes are quicker, but a first-hand account calls double ropes here annoying and prone to sticking and prefers a single 70 m, and a single 60 m does not reach the only bolted anchor on the route. The approximate lengths, about 40, 55, 55, 40 and 60 m, come from the North Face descent description.
wa_ultramega_ok.descent_text: Ultramega OK has no independent, well-established rappel line of its own — it is a Northeast Buttress route whose last pitch finishes up an offwidth crack to the summit, though a party that loses the line high up can traverse ledges into upper North Face terrain (near Burgundy Ledge) and finish from there. From wherever the route is topped out, the standard way down is the North Face's 5-rappel descent: ~40m from a heavily slung summit boulder down the middle of the upper face to a bolted ledge anchor; ~55m from the bolts down lichen-covered rock to a huge ledge near a rock arch (traverse the ledge to a constriction with slings); ~55m from that constriction down to a blue-slung horn; ~40m from the horn to broad scree ledges (watch the rope pull here — lots of snag potential); and a final ~60m back to Burgundy Col. Double 60m ropes make this clean; parties with a single 70m have reported getting down with some downclimbing between stances, but it's tighter on this line than on the standard North Face. From the base of the raps, reverse the Burgundy Col approach back to the highway. A few parties describe instead downclimbing loose 3rd/4th-class terrain on Burgundy's east side back toward the col to avoid rappelling altogether, but this is opportunistic route-finding rather than an established descent, and is not recommended in the wet or for parties unfamiliar with the terrain.

wa_cascade_peak_east_ridge.rappels: Rappel the NW Chimney back to the moat on double ropes, building anchors from slung horns, chockstones and your own gear: there is no fixed hardware, and what tat exists is poor. No count is published; plan on several rappels, then reverse the CJ Couloir.
wa_cascade_peak_east_ridge.rappel_count_note: No party has published a rappel count or station list for this descent, so none is shown. Expect to build every anchor yourself in the NW Chimney, bring doubles for full-length rappels, and carry cord to leave behind.
wa_cascade_peak_east_ridge.descent_text: From the summit, downclimb/simul-climb back to the top of the technical pitches, then rappel the NW Chimney back down to the moat using gear anchors you build as you go (bring doubles for full-length raps -- there is no fixed hardware on this route). Traverse back to the C-J col and reverse the CJ Couloir (roughly 3,400 ft of downclimbing/rappelling on snow and ice) to the base near the Cascade River, then retrace the short bushwhack and road walk to the trailhead. Avoid the Doug Direct descent some older references mention off the col -- a firsthand trip report calls it a slower, no-safer heather-and-rock traverse than simply reversing the couloir.

ut_kor_ingalls_route.rappels: Descent from the north face takes four raps on one 70 m rope, or two on a pair of 70 m ropes.

wa_cathedral_rock_northeast_buttress.rappels: No established rappel descent; the route is descended by the south side. Doubled-up 50m ropes have been used, which also gives a full-length rappel capability for bailing off the buttress or for the one to two rappels on the Southwest Face descent.

wa_cathedral_rock_northeast_ridge_2003_v.rappels: No established rappel line; descend the south side. Carry spare slings and rings to build bail anchors if you need to retreat off the lower pitches. Doubled ropes make retreat from mid-route far more practical.
